name: Sunbathing / tanmaxxing

card.summary: Getting a tan with sun, lamps or sunless products for a healthier-looking complexion; tans are a documented skin-damage response.
card.note: WHO, the American Cancer Society and the US Surgeon General warn against excessive sun and indoor tanning; sunless tanning products avoid UV.

quick.overview:
Tanmaxxing is the community term for tanning to improve how the skin looks, whether by sunbathing, tanning products or sunless alternatives. Tanned skin has been fashionable in the West since the 1920s, and looksmaxxing guides treat colour as part of skin and overall appearance.

Research on UV exposure documents an association with sunburn, photoaging and skin cancer, and expert guidance generally cautions against UV tanning. Sunless self-tanners using dihydroxyacetone are described as a way to darken skin without UV.
quick.mechanism: UV radiation prompts melanocytes to make melanin. UVA darkens existing pigment through oxidative stress, while UVB causes DNA damage that triggers new melanin production and a tan that appears a few days later. Sunless tanners react with proteins in the outer skin layer to produce a brown colour.
quick.risks: Excess UV is associated with sunburn, DNA mutations, skin cancer, accelerated skin ageing and immune suppression. A 2010 study linked frequent tanning bed use to about triple the melanoma risk. Skin type matters: people with fair skin burn more easily.

lead: Tanmaxxing is looksmaxxing slang for darkening the skin, by sunbathing, tanning oils and lotions, tanning devices or sunless products, to look healthier or more attractive. Tanning itself is the skin's pigment response to ultraviolet radiation.[1]

Research and public-health bodies document that UV exposure is associated with sunburn, skin ageing and skin cancer, and organisations including the WHO, the American Cancer Society and the US Surgeon General warn against excessive sun and indoor tanning exposure.[1][2] Sun exposure also supports vitamin D production.[1] Sunless products based on dihydroxyacetone darken the skin without UV.[1]

paras: Before the 1920s in the US and Western Europe, tanned skin signalled outdoor labour and lower class, and upper classes used parasols and covering clothing. Sunlight was promoted as therapy in the early 1900s; Niels Finsen received the 1903 Nobel Prize in Medicine for light therapy.[1] Tans became fashionable in the 1920s, with Coco Chanel's Riviera tan widely imitated, and Jean Patou launched the first sun tan oil in 1927.[1] SPF ratings began in 1962, and tanning beds appeared from 1978.[1]

Melanocytes produce melanin, either red pheomelanin or dark brown eumelanin. UVA darkens existing melanin quickly through oxidative stress and fades, while UVB causes direct DNA damage that triggers new melanin production, yielding a tan after two to three days that offers modest protection, roughly equivalent to SPF 3. The Fitzpatrick scale from 1975 classifies skin types I to VI by burning and tanning tendency.[1]

A reference source lists moderate sun exposure as supporting vitamin D synthesis, and excess UV as causing sunburn, DNA mutations, skin cancer, photoaging and immune suppression.[1] A 2024 expert review states that in fair-skinned populations up to 95 percent of keratinocyte skin cancers and 70 to 95 percent of cutaneous melanomas are caused by ultraviolet radiation.[2] Photodamage begins early in childhood, with 50 to 80 percent of lifetime UV exposure occurring before age 18, according to a 1999 review.[3]

A Danish study of sun seekers on a one-week holiday examined sunburn rates during sunbathing.[4] Earlier case-control research found increased melanoma risk with severe sunburn before age 15 and with sunbathing.[5] The sources describe UVA exposure as triggering beta-endorphin release, and a small 2006 trial reported withdrawal-like symptoms in frequent tanners given an opioid blocker.[1]
Guidance summarised in reference sources says to avoid sunburn, to use sunscreen, to recognise that a tan is a response to DNA damage, and to consider sunless alternatives.[1]

Self-tanners, gels, lotions and sprays with dihydroxyacetone darken skin without UV, bronzers give temporary cosmetic colour, and professional spray tanning uses a colourless chemical that reacts with proteins in the outer skin layer.[1] A nationwide survey has profiled users of sunless tanning products.[6]
No studies found testing tanning for attractiveness or looks outcomes. Human studies instead address sunburn behaviour, skin cancer risk, photoaging and vitamin D, as summarised above.[2][4][5]

A looksmax.org guide describes tanning with the sun as the basic method, recommends products such as tanning oils and lotions with SPF, and also covers ways to get colour without the sun.[7] Looksmaxxing guides treat colour as one component of skin and overall presentation.

timeline.event: Niels Finsen wins the Nobel Prize in Medicine for light therapy.[1]
Tanned skin becomes fashionable in the West.[1]
Health authorities ban psoralen in tanning activators.[1]

lore.intro: Tanmaxxing guides on looksmax.org present tanning, with sun and with products, as part of skin optimisation.[7]

claims.claim: A good tan improves how the skin looks and can be done cleanly with the right products.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org guide says tans build gradually, that tanning oils and lotions with SPF help the skin pick up colour evenly, and that sunless options exist for colour without roasting in the sun.[7]
claims.experts: Reference sources describe a tan as the skin's response to UV-induced DNA damage and recommend sunburn avoidance and sunless alternatives; no study has measured effects on perceived attractiveness.[1][2]
